With the offseason here for the Boston Red Sox, it's going to be interesting to see where the club looks to add throughout the winter.
At first glance, the most obvious areas to add seemingly would be power through the designated hitter spot, potentially a left-handed reliever and maybe a right-handed starting pitcher, depending on what happens with Sonny Gray. This is on paper, though. It doesn't necessarily mean that this is what the Red Sox are looking for. The offseason is long and unpredictable.
Catcher is a spot that was discussed over and over again, but Boston struck and acquired Adley Rutschman ahead of the trade deadline and he's under team control for the 2027 season. It would seem that catcher is set with Rutschman and Connor Wong, but one thing that is interesting is the fact that WEEI's Rob Bradford reported that the Red Sox made a run at Hunter Feduccia ahead of the trade deadline, although they missed out as the Los Angeles Dodgers got him.
"The Red Sox were also really trying to get another catcher at the deadline (as well as Adley): Hunter Feduccia," Bradford wrote.
The Red Sox Looked To Add Another Catcher
Feduccia played in 33 games for the Dodgers and slashed .197/.322/.263 with one home run and seven RBIs. Surprisingly, those numbers are actually better than Wong's down the stretch. After the trade deadline, Wong slashed .188/.222/.319 with two home runs and eight RBIs in 22 games played.
At the end of the day, on paper the Red Sox should be set behind the plate with Rutschman leading the charge behind the plate and Wong under team control. Plus, of course, Mickey Gasper could be an option, if Boston saw fit. But if the trade deadline interest is any indication, it would appear as though the backup catcher spot could be something to watch this winter as well.
Last year, the Red Sox looked around and brought in Matt Thaiss to compete for the backup spot with Wong. The 30-year-old won the job over Thaiss and did a good job throughout the 2026 season overall. His offensive numbers weren't great down the stretch, but he batted .233 on the season and was very good with the pitching staff.
Still, while backup catcher may not be an obvious need for the club, it's something to monitor throughout the offseason. It's going to be a long winter. By the end of it, the roster isn't going to look exactly the same — in both obvious and non-obvious ways. Regardless of what happens, hopefully we're able to see baseball in full force on time for Spring Training.

item.content:encoded:
You get what’s shaping up to be pretty much the best pitching matchup you could ask for in Game 1 of the NL Championship Series.
The Dodgers announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will get the ball in Game 1 on Sunday, and while the Brewers haven't made anything official, they are in prime position to have ace Jacob Misiorowski on the mound. Both teams clinched their spot in the NLCS on Thursday, the Brewers with a 3-1 win over the Padres and the Dodgers with a 4-1 win over the Braves.
Misiorowski pitched just once in the series, throwing four innings of two-run ball in Game 1. Similarly, Skubal opened things against the Braves, going six innings with just one run allowed, and did not pitch again. Both should be well-rested.
The most realistic argument against a Skubal-Misiorowski duel lies in October superstar Yoshinobu Yamamoto, but the Dodgers righty pitched in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday, meaning he’d start Sunday on just four days’ rest. He will pitch in Game 2 on Monday with a regular recovery that would make more sense.
We’ve seen great pitching in the 2026 postseason thus far and several marquee matchups: Cam Schlittler vs. Payton Tolle; Chris Sale vs. Jesús Luzardo; Max Fried vs. Sonny Gray; Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen; Yamamoto vs. Sale.
If it happens, Skubal vs. Misiorowski will take the cake.
After some struggles late in the regular season, Misiorowski pitched behind an opener when he made his postseason debut a year ago, but he was effective in three appearances. He allowed only one run across seven innings in the NLDS against the Cubs, before striking out nine and yielding just one run in five innings against the Dodgers in the NLCS.
But this is not the same Miz in 2026. The flame-throwing 24-year-old finished the regular season with MLB bests in ERA (1.80), strikeouts (252), WHIP (0.80) and opponents’ batting average (.157). It was more than a breakout -- it was among the greatest pitching seasons in MLB history.
Misiorowski’s four-seam fastball topped out at 104.8 mph and averaged 101.2 mph against the Padres in the NLDS. With the adrenaline that is sure to be present on Sunday, who knows what eye-popping numbers he could put up.
As for Skubal, he won’t win a third consecutive Cy Young. But that won’t take away from the 2.72 ERA he posted in 26 starts, including a 2.61 mark after his blockbuster trade to the Dodgers. Remember, too, that Skubal missed 44 days in the summer after he needed surgery to remove loose bodies in his left elbow. There have been few signs of rust from that recovery.
Skubal’s strong playoff debut with the Dodgers was just more of what we’re used to from the southpaw. He made six postseason starts as a Tiger in 2024 and 2025 with a 2.04 ERA, never going shorter than six innings and allowing more than two runs just once.
The Brewers and Dodgers will already provide appointment viewing throughout the NLCS, a rematch of the 2025 NL pennant battle and a meeting of MLB’s top regular-season teams in 2026. Add in the potential bout of Misiorowski and Skubal in Game 1, and this series should get off to an awfully hot start.

item.content:encoded:
One thing that Boston Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow has shown multiple times since taking over the organization is that he's not afraid to make a splash in the trade market.
If you look at the Red Sox's 2026 roster, you'll notice a handful of guys were added by way of trade. Garrett Crochet, Sonny Gray, Erik Miller, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Curtis Mead, Andruw Monasterio, Caleb Durbin, Eli White and Willson Contreras, among others. The trade market has been Boston's avenue of choice to improve and nothing should be ruled out this winter. Sure, Boston's farm system isn't as good as it was a few years ago, in large part due to the trades, as well as promotions to the big leagues. But there are still plenty of pieces that could be used to bring talent to town this winter.
Arguably, the perfect fit would be Bryce Harper of the Philadelphia Phillies. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and USA Today's Bob Nightengale both have insinuated that Harper could be floated by the Phillies this offseason as a potential trade chip, if he is willing to waive his no-trade clause. We already have made the case for why he would be a great fit for Boston. But what could an actual trade look like? Here's a mock trade both sides should consider.
Red Sox Receive: OF/1B Bryce Harper
Phillies Receive: OF Jarren Duran, INF/OF Kristian Campbell, SP Tanner Houck
It's important to note that this is a mock trade. It's far more difficult to actually get a deal done, rather than talking about the idea. When it comes to Harper, the most important variables are whether the Phillies actually would be interested in trading the two-time MVP and then whether he would even be willing to waive his no-trade clause. If the answer to both of those questions was, "yes." Then, you could proceed.
The Phillies notably had a shaky outfield in 2026, plus Adolis Garcia is heading to free agency. Duran had a tough 2026 season, but this is also a guy who had 9.0 wins above replacement in 2024 and 4.9 wins above replacement in 2025. There are reasons to believe that he could get back to that level. Campbell would be the jewel of the deal. He's just 24 years old and already has a long-term deal. He could play in the outfield, or replace Luis Arraez in the infield.
When it comes to Houck, he's someone who is healthy now and who was an All-Star in his last full season in 2024. He got hurt in 2025 and missed all of the 2026 season, except the regular season finale. Still, he could either help in the rotation, or in the bullpen. Houck was selected in the first round of the MLB Draft in 2017, when Dave Dombrowski was still Boston's president of baseball operations.
Again, the idea of a Harper deal is a pipe dream right now. If the Phillies shop him and he is willing to waive his no-trade clause, then this could be more realistic. But there are also finances involved. He has five years left on his deal and will make just over $27 million in 2027 and 2028. Then, he'll make just over $23 million in each of the final three seasons. Are the Red Sox willing to take on that type of money? It would be better than spending something similar on Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki.

Sonny Gray pitched a great game against the New York Yankees in Wild Card Game 2. Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning despite the single run he'd allowed at that point and the Boston Red Sox crumbled from there.
During the game, some fans noticed some brown flecks on the right side of Gray's neck, on the same side as his pitching arm. Speculation about cheating ran rampant on social media despite the veteran passing all his in-game hand and glove checks from the umpires.
Chris Cotillo on October 6 reported that MLB investigated Gray for the potential use of illegal substances. Since Gray has not been officially disciplined by the league and he passed all the in-game examinations, Cotillo assumes he's in the clear.
While it was evident that Gray had something on his neck, it didn't look like pine tar, which can be seen in dark, glossy layers on players' helmets and bats. in April 2024, Yankees pitcher Michael Pineda was ejected for using pine tar, which he rubbed on his neck before the game, to improve his grip on the ball. The pine tar was in a uniform smear on his neck and not pilled up, as whatever was on Gray's neck appeared.
MLB investigated Red Sox's Sonny Gray for rumors of illegal sticky substance use in Wild Card Game 2 against Yankees
If there was something sticky on Gray's neck that remained there after he rubbed his fingers over it before nearly every batter, it would remain on his hands when he presented them to umpires to be checked after every inning.
It wasn't even unique for Gray to touch his neck before every pitch — he's been seen doing the same swiping motion on the side of his neck countless times. Using sweat to increase the stickiness of rosin on one's hands, a completely legal substance, is a trick used by pitchers throughout the league over many years.
Gray was the Sox's ace all season and he gave his teammates a great start in the postseason without cheating. His 2.72 ERA over 169 innings this season and 1.98 ERA in two starts against the Yankees aren't indicative of someone who needs extra, illegal help to get through games.
Gray is an impending free agent and the Sox's 2027 rotation will miss him dearly. He was the only righty in the rotation and his 18 wins matched Garrett Crochet's total in 2025. Both pitchers were incredibly effective stoppers in their full seasons with Boston.
Gray's tenure with the Red Sox didn't end on the best note, as he was dissatisfied with Tracy's decision to pull him so early in the game. But if Boston seeks a reunion with Gray, it can do so in good conscience, knowing he didn't use illegal substances in a playoff game.

In the immediate aftermath of the Red Sox’s season-ending loss to the Yankees in Game 2 of last week’s Wild Card Series, both Willson Contreras and Sonny Gray — two of the club’s most respected veteran leaders — expressed frustration with the way decisions were being made by the organization.
During Monday’s hour-long year-end press conference, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy said they’d met with both players to help clear the air.
Breslow said he and Tracy both spoke to Contreras for two hours on Sunday, covering a wide range of topics. Breslow wouldn’t delve into specifics but described the conversations as productive while pushing back on the notion that Contreras wants things fixed and changed.
“We had a great conversation, Trace and I, with Willson yesterday, we met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things, many of those I will keep private to preserve the relationship that we have,” Breslow said. “But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things, and Willson would be the right person to ask directly but he spoke very very highly of his time here and how much he’s looking forward to 2027 and the way he and his family appreciated the Red Sox.”
Tracy said he spoke to Gray as well and, while the veteran understandably disagreed with his decision to pull him in the fifth inning of Wednesday’s loss, their relationship is in a good place.
“I didn’t suspect most starters, especially in that case, guys are going to be happy about being pulled. I thought he answered the questions that were asked of him in a very professional manner and yes, I have had a chance to talk to him. The relationship there is good,” Tracy said. “Do I think he was wanting to stay out there? Quite obviously. But five months of relationship building with players and I think there’s some things that get painted sometimes that that’s stained it or ruined it and I have a very good working relationship with him and I’ve had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year. But yeah I was able to talk to him, it’s in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings on it.”
Both Gray and Contreras expressed unhappiness about Tracy’s decision to pull the starter early, with Gray telling reporters postgame that he would have “liked to have been trusted in that moment” while Contreras simply zipped his lips when asked.
Contreras was willing to speak more directly on his frustration with the club’s heavy reliance on data and analytics, saying that ultimately teams need experience and veteran players to win games.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game,” Contreras said last week. “You have to do a lot of different stuff, and it’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that’s telling you what to do. Because this is baseball. And the data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you’re gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games. And yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but not saying.”

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)

The aftermath of the Red Sox's postseason exit against the Yankees led to some clear frustration in the clubhouse.
As Boston began reflecting on its quick exit in the AL Wild Card Round, veteran pitcher Sonny Gray's comments about his exit in Game 2 of the series particularly caught fans' attention, expressing frustration that he was pulled after 4.2 innings.
On Monday, during the Red Sox's end-of-season press conference, manager Chad Tracy addressed Gray's comments for the first time.
Here's what Tracy said in response to Gray's frustration about being pulled early in Game 2.
Chad Tracy Addresses Sonny Gray's Comments About Early Game 2 Exit
Last week, following the Red Sox's Game 2 loss to the Yankees, Gray was vocal about his desire to continue pitching in the spot when he was pulled.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact," Gray said. "I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. I think you can probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted. But what can you do?
"I would have liked to been trusted in that moment."

— NESN (@NESN) October 1, 2026
On Monday, Tracy was asked about his decision to pull Gray in Game 2 and his thoughts on the veteran pitcher's comments.
The Red Sox manager said that he would "suspect" most pitchers would not want to leave the game under those circumstances, but he has spoken with Gray since then.
"Didn't suspect most starters, especially in that case, that guys are gonna be happy with being pulled," Tracy said. "Was able to talk to him, it's in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings on it."
Tracy also said he has a "very good working relationship" with Gray.

When looking back on his pitching decisions in the Yankees series, Tracy said he'd "push back" on Gray's stance about him being the best option for a third turn through the order.
"It's a combination of what matchups can you create, who's in the bullpen, what am I thinking here, are we winning or losing," Tracy said. "You're factoring all those things."

CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

Boston Red Sox right-hander Sonny Gray didn't get the final start of the season he wanted against the New York Yankees, though several factors contributed.

All he can look forward to is the future, though many questions remain about whether his future will be in Major League Baseball.
Gray has talked about possibly retiring, as the soon-to-be 37-year-old in November faces a major decision about his future in Major League Baseball.
Rumors of his retirement have been circulating, and Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet had a lot to say about it.
"I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose," Crochet said, according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo. "Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
A lot of these guys understand that getting family time is very important, but as Crochet touched on, he still has a lot to give to this game.
Gray's a three-time All-Star and was arguably the best pitcher in the American League for a lot of the season this year. He ended up with an 18-5 record, leading the American League in wins.
He also posted a 2.72 ERA and struck out 149 hitters in 169.0 innings.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – How the Yankees' Bay State duo of Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice performed in the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox – drafted out of Massachusetts – was also a take-a-bow moment for player development.
"Just impressive to see these young guys step into the biggest stage at the biggest moment,'' said Yankees captain Aaron Judge, their supreme first-round pick (32nd overall) from the 2013 draft.
Here's a look at the other Yankees drafted and developed players who could impact the best-of-five Division Series against the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays:
George Lombard Jr.
Age: 21
Yankees draft info: 1st round (26th overall) in 2023.
In his first taste of postseason – with 42 games of MLB experience – the shortstop handled his position well and went 4-for-8 at the plate.
"A couple of years ago, he was playing high school baseball,'' Judge said of Lombard, while praising the Yanks' rookie and sophomore class in general.
"Just a really good player,'' Max Fried said of Lombard Jr. "He's got a slow heartbeat.''
Spencer Jones
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (25th overall) in 2022.
Despite Trent Grisham's return, Jones – who batted .389/1.107 OPS in 59 MLB plate appearances vs. lefties – started in center field against Payton Tolle in the Wild Card opener.
The lefty-hitting Jones was shifted to right field vs. Sonny Gray in Game 2, batting cleanup, with Grisham in center.
Jones went 2-for-8 with a walk and four strikeouts in the ALWC.
Judge's status could impact his late game at-bats, if the captain is on the roster, but the 6-foot-7 slugger has earned his opportunity as a regular in postseason.
Ben Rice
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 12th round in 2021.
Rice destroyed the Red Sox in the Yanks' 9-0, Wild Card Series Game 1 win, with two homers - including a grand slam - among his four hits, with six RBI as the DH.
With 41 homers this year, Rice joined Judge as the only drafted Yankees to reach the 40-homer mark in a single regular season.
Expect Rice to continue batting leadoff against the Rays' right-handed starters. Also, he's a .458 hitter with five homers and a 1.685 OPS in seven career games at the Trop.
Anthony Volpe
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (30th overall) in 2019.
Volpe started the Wild Card opener vs. the lefty Tolle, going 1-for-3 at second base, a new MLB position for him upon his return; he was optioned to Triple-A with Lombard's early August call-up.
Lefty-hitting Jazz Chisholm Jr., on the bench in WC Game 1, started Game 2 vs. the right-handed Gray and went 2-for-3 with a walk in a clinching 9-2 victory.
Given the Rays' right-handed rotation, Volpe might be a bench player this series, utilized later in games for his infield versatility (including some third base) and as a pinch-runner.
Cam Schlittler
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 7th round in 2022.
Red Sox Nation has already seen enough postseason Schlittler, helping take Boston out of the last two AL Wild Card Series.
After his 117-pitch scoreless effort in Tuesday's Wild Card opener, Schlittler gets the ball in Monday's ALDS Game 2, on one extra day of rest.
That also puts him in line for a possible Game 5 on normal rest. Both games are at Trop, and Schlittler owns a 1.16 ERA in 17 road starts this year.
Will Warren
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 8th round in 2021.
Moved into a multi-inning relief role in postseason, Warren tossed 1.2 innings (one run) following Fried in Game 2.
He should fit that same role against the Rays, with the ability to take over for a shaky or injured starter, or to provide a bridge to the high-leverage duo of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick, leading into David Bednar.
Austin Wells
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 1st round (28th overall) in 2020.
At the plate, the lefty-hitting Wells picked it up considerably after a brutal first four months, but his value behind the plate - and his knack for ABS challenges - has been a constant.
As for defending the speedy, daring Rays, "they love to run and take advantage,'' said Wells, emphasizing the limiting of walks in this series.
Wells has been paired all year with Game 1 starter Gerrit Cole, who praised the "role Austin has played in run prevention'' for a staff that led the league in ERA.

The New York Yankees came away with an easy two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round of the American League playoffs.
The Yankees did exactly what they had to do on both sides of the baseball, completely dominating Boston when it came to the pitching side of things.
Offensively speaking, the Yankees were just as great, scoring a combined 18 runs, putting up nine in each contest. The Yankees were able to do a lot of good in Wednesday night's win, but a lot of that was questioned afterward by some of the players on the Red Sox. Some players clearly didn't feel like Sonny Gray should have been pulled, including Gray, who only threw 4.2 innings, allowing six hits and two earned runs.
Gray didn't walk any and struck out five. After coming out of the game, the Yankees offense was able to get going, putting together great at-bats against Erik Miller, Garrett Crochet, and Garrett Whitlock. As a whole, the three only pitched 1.2 innings, allowing eight hits and seven runs.
Willson Contreras and Gray had a lot to say about why they believed that shouldn't have been the case after the game.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do," Contreras said. "Because this is baseball, and the data is here to help us, but at the end of the day we're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time; I think that's a fact," said Gray, per The Athletic.
"Yeah, I mean, I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted. But what can you do, you know?"
As a competitor, it's not crazy to think Gray is right in a scenario like this.
It didn't feel like he had to be taken out in that scenario, but a lot of skippers and other decision-makers around Major League Baseball take guys out in moments like that when they're going through a lineup for the third time. It's one of those things that can either come back to haunt a team or be the right decision.
I'm personally not the biggest fan of not allowing Gray to stay on the mound, but that's just my opinion. It obviously worked out for the Yankees, but this was another time that showed that maybe a team should have trusted its gut instead of listening to an iPad.

NUEVA YORK — Los Red Sox de Boston aguantaron dos noches en el Bronx. Las discusiones que dejaron atrás siguen en marcha.
Los Yankees arrasaron en la Serie de Comodín de la Liga Americana en el Yankee Stadium, ganando 9-0 el martes y 9-2 el miércoles. Boston anotó dos carreras en 18 entradas.
Nueva York lo consiguió sin Aaron Judge. Max Fried y Cam Schlittler mantuvieron a los Red Sox a una sola carrera en 12 1/3 entradas. El jonrón de tres carreras de Cody Bellinger en una séptima entrada en la que se anotaron seis carreras acabó con cualquier duda en el segundo partido. Antes, Luis García Jr. rompió el empate a cero con un jonrón en la cuarta entrada ante Sonny Gray, y el as de Boston, Garrett Crochet, no consiguió eliminar a ninguno de los cuatro bateadores a los que se enfrentó.
La temporada de Boston había dado un giro radical. Los Red Sox despidieron al entrenador Alex Cora durante una racha que les dejó 14 partidos por debajo del 50 % a finales de junio. Respondieron con una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4 —récord de la franquicia— para alcanzar el puesto n.º 5.
Los Yankees han eliminado ahora a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez. Nueva York lleva una ventaja de 4-3 en los siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, con victorias en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026.
Boston anotó cinco carreras en sus últimos cuatro partidos de playoffs contra los Yankees, todos disputados en el Bronx. El jonrón de Willson Contreras en el segundo partido puso fin a una sequía anotadora de los Red Sox en la postemporada de 26 2/3 entradas.
La mayoría de los años, la conversación pasaría directamente a la siguiente ronda. Esta vez, se fue por otros derroteros.
La temporada de Boston se había convertido en tema de conversación mucho más allá del Fenway Park. Una senadora estadounidense que luchaba por su supervivencia política había vinculado parte de su discurso a ella. Un magnate de los medios nacido en Massachusetts con millones de seguidores estaba dispuesto a defenderla.
El jueves por la mañana, ambos tuvieron que rendir cuentas ante un equipo de los Yankees que les había endosado un 18-2.
Un anuncio de campaña que apostaba por Boston
La senadora republicana Susan Collins, de Maine, aspira a un sexto mandato. Su campaña emitió un anuncio que utilizaba la rivalidad para enmarcar su contienda contra el líder de la minoría del Senado, Chuck Schumer, un demócrata de Nueva York y conocido seguidor de los Yankees.
El anuncio alterna entre imágenes del Fenway Park, un Schumer serio y Collins saludando a los votantes por todo Maine. La frase inicial parecía un informe de seguimiento sobre los Yankees.
«Los Red Sox saben cómo lidiar con los Yankees, y Susan Collins sabe cómo lidiar con Chuck Schumer, el súper fan de los Yankees», dice el narrador.
A continuación, el anuncio pasa del béisbol a la lealtad al estado natal. Presenta el equipo al que anima Schumer como prueba de cuáles son sus prioridades.
«Mientras Chuck Schumer anima a Nueva York, el equipo de Susan es Maine», dice el narrador.
Schumer es un blanco habitual de Collins porque los grupos demócratas vinculados a él han gastado mucho dinero en campaña contra ella. Una organización sin ánimo de lucro afiliada al Senate Majority PAC, vinculado a Schumer, invirtió 2 millones de dólares en anuncios contra Collins a principios de este año, según Axios.
Schumer responde a la guerra de anuncios contra los Yankees
Schumer tomó la palabra la mañana después de que se aseguraran el título. Cuando le preguntaron por la serie, se centró en la premisa del anuncio.
«No fueron los Yankees los que se quedaron en blanco las dos últimas noches», dijo Schumer.
El rival demócrata de Collins tampoco se libró de la serie. Troy Jackson, ex presidente del Senado de Maine y leñador del norte del estado, publicó su apoyo a Boston antes del primer partido.
«¡Vamos, Sox!», escribió Jackson en X.
La maniobra innecesaria de Portnoy
La segunda voz de Boston llegó tras el último out. El fundador de Barstool Sports, Dave Portnoy, natural de Massachusetts y seguidor de toda la vida de los Red Sox, vio cómo los Yankees celebraban en su vestuario y publicó su veredicto en X.
Portnoy se centró en la fiesta, no en el resultado. Las celebraciones con champán son habituales tras ganar una serie en la MLB, algo que una nota de la comunidad de X añadió más tarde a su publicación.
«Que los Yankees celebren con champán la victoria en la serie de comodines solo demuestra lo bajo que ha caído esa franquicia. Es muy vergonzoso», escribió Portnoy.
Un usuario sugirió que Portnoy publica una versión de la misma queja cada otoño.
«El tuit programado de cada año, jajaja. Seguro que programaste este el año pasado porque sabías que volvería a pasar», escribió un usuario de X.
En cifras: una primicia en la historia de octubre de esta rivalidad
Esta barrida le dio a Nueva York algo que nunca había conseguido contra Boston. Los Yankees han eliminado a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez.
En siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, Nueva York lleva la delantera por 4-3, tras ganar en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026. Boston ganó en 2004, 2018 y en el partido de comodín de 2021.
En los últimos cuatro partidos de postemporada entre estos rivales, todos disputados en el Bronx, los Red Sox anotaron cinco carreras.
La temporada regular había apuntado en otra dirección. Boston encadenó una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4, récord de la franquicia, pero Nueva York se llevó la serie de la temporada por 7-6, coronada con una goleada de 16-1 en el último encuentro.
Los Rays son los siguientes, mientras la carrera por Maine sigue reñida
Los Yankees descansan dos días antes del primer partido de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana contra los Tampa Bay Rays, campeones de la División Este de la Liga Americana. El primer lanzamiento está previsto para las 18:30 h EDT del sábado en el Tropicana Field.
Tampa Bay tenía el mejor balance de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees acabaron con un balance de 6-7 contra los Rays durante la temporada regular. La disponibilidad de Judge sigue siendo la mayor incógnita en torno a la alineación y la plantilla del entrenador Aaron Boone.
Una encuesta de CNN/SSRS realizada a 880 votantes registrados, entre el 31 de agosto y el 6 de septiembre, mostró que Jackson iba por delante de Collins con un 48 % frente a un 45 %. El «Cook Political Report» califica la contienda como reñida.
Los dos candidatos sí que comparten una cosa: los dos son seguidores de los Red Sox.
La temporada de Boston ya ha terminado. La racha de los Yankees continúa este sábado en San Petersburgo, Florida. Los votantes de Maine acudirán a las urnas el 3 de noviembre.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

The Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, and Sonny Gray now faces a decision on his future.
Earlier this year, the 36-year-old pitcher noted that he is open to retiring if his family wants him to hang it up. He had a great year and revealed after the game that he thinks he has a lot of baseball left in him. However, he needs to decide if playing is what's best for him and his family.
"I was telling him that a second ago, whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year," ace Garrett Crochet said after the loss to the Yankees, per MassLive's Chris Cotillo. "I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
Even if Gray continues to play, his postgame comments open the door for him to leave the Red Sox. He has a $30 million mutual option, which will likely be declined by the Red Sox. He could re-sign as a free agent, but when he was asked if Boston was a destination he would consider after the year he had, he said "I don't know."
Gray stepped up big time for the Red Sox this year. They needed the entire rotation to play better with Crochet hurt. Having him and Crochet together in the rotation, along with Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez, would be great for the Red Sox.

The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove.
In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001.
But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention.
Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to the ALDS.
“I’m able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said afterward, reflecting on sharing the night with his father. “That was a cool moment, just a great game. Happy I was able to contribute, and we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Continued contributions from Bellinger would go a long way in the Yankees making a deep postseason run, with the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays up next in the ALDS.
Bellinger takes on added importance with Aaron Judge sidelined indefinitely due to a calf strain.
He was one of the driving forces in the Yankees’ two-day demolition of the archrival Red Sox, whom they outscored 18-2. The All-Star went 3-for-8 in the series and delivered a pair of key hits in Wednesday’s clincher.
With Yankees leading by a run in the fifth inning, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy controversially removed right-handed starter Sonny Gray after 70 pitches with runners at the corners and two outs.
Tracy turned to the left-handed Erik Miller to face the lefty-swinging Bellinger, who delivered an RBI single that put the Yankees up, 2-0.
Then in the sixth, after an intentional walk to Ben Rice in front of him, Bellinger capped a six-run rally with a three-run home run against right-handed reliever Garrett Whitlock — a 360-foot drive into the right-field stands that served as the dagger.
“He’s built for this,” Judge said Wednesday during a champagne-soaked celebration in the Yankees clubhouse. “He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment, and he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Bellinger, who won the 2019 National League MVP and the 2020 World Series with the Los Angeles Dodgers, is in his second season with the Yankees, having re-signed last winter on a five-year, $162.5 million contract.
Despite missing a month with a hamstring strain, Bellinger batted .264 with 17 home runs, 73 RBI and a .768 OPS in 132 games. He was worth 4.6 WAR (wins above replacement), in part because of his excellent defensive work in left field, too.
“This offseason, there were a couple of other teams involved,” Clay Bellinger said in August of his son’s free agency. “But I said, ‘If you can sign back with these guys, and you go out there and you win a world championship to add to this legacy, there’s no better place in the world to play baseball.’”
The elder Bellinger would know, as the former utility player won World Series with the Yankees in 1999 and 2000.
Now, the Yankees’ World Series aspirations rest in large part with Bellinger, who continues to carve out his own pinstriped legacy.
Despite hitting left-handed, Bellinger is actually better against left-handed pitching than he is against righties, making his bat even more crucial for balance in a Judge-less lineup that’s loaded with lefties.
The Yankees went 15-for-35 (.429) against left-handers in the Red Sox series, with Bellinger recording two hits in those matchups and another top-of-the-order lefty batter in Rice totaling three.
“No secret sauce,” Bellinger said of his reverse splits. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. Felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, didn’t hear too much about the match-ups. I was just playing baseball.”
After hitting .214 in his first postseason with the Yankees, Bellinger is off to a .333 start to this one. Wednesday’s home run was Bellinger’s 11th in the postseason and his second in nine playoff games with the Yankees.
“I feel like I was able to enjoy that one,” Bellinger said. “Just a home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play. And hopefully we get many, many more this month.”

La segunda jornada de la Serie de Comodín en la temporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) selló el adiós de los dos cubanos más mediáticos de la Liga Americana: el slugger Yordan Álvarez y el lanzador Aroldis Chapman.
Los Astros de Houston, de los que Yordan fue bujía a lo largo de la campaña, cayeron en apenas dos juegos ante los Medias Blancas de Chicago, mientras a los Medias Rojas de Chapman los frenaron en seco uno de los exequipos del cerrador holguinero: los Yankees en Nueva York.
Los Medias Blancas ganaron este miércoles 7-3 en Houston y completaron la barrida sobre los Astros. Así, dejaron sin opciones al tunero de seguir ensanchando la mejor campaña de su trayectoria, coronada con el liderazgo de bateo del circuito con promedio de .316, además de despachar 42 jonrones y luchar por la Triple Corona hasta el final del calendario regular.
Houston, we don’t have a problem pic.twitter.com/NmPM6SCndJ
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) October 1, 2026
Poco pudo aportar Yordan a la causa, al irse en blanco en cuatro visitas al plato. Con ello dejó su producción ofensiva en la postemporada en solo un imparable en los ocho turnos oficiales sumados por él en los dos choques disputados.
La suerte estuvo siempre del lado visitante, pues Chicago anotó cuatro veces en el primer episodio ante el abridor Hunter Brown, ayudado por errores defensivos. En lo adelante, los Astros solo pudieron responder con jonrones solitarios de José Altuve, Jeremy Peña y Cam Smith.
Este duelo era el de mayores expectativas entre los aficionados cubanos dada la presencia en el bando de Chicago del joven antesalista Miguel Vargas, quien tuvo su mejor temporada en la fase preliminar, pero no ha tenido un feliz estreno en la instancia decisiva.
El habanero volvió a fallar en cinco turnos, lo que, unido a un similar desempeño en el choque anterior, lo mantiene a la espera de su primer imparable en la postemporada.
Esta vez el protagonismo recayó en Chase Meidroth, autor de un vuelacercas de tres carreras, y en el bullpen encabezado por Erick Fedde y Jordan Hicks, quienes no permitieron hits en cuatro entradas combinadas para apuntalar la victoria de Anthony Kay.
3-RUN POSTSEASON HOMER FOR CHASE MEIDROTH! pic.twitter.com/39yNEWjiLt
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) September 30, 2026
Boston desarmado
En el Yankee Stadium, los dueños de casa complacieron a sus parciales con la segunda victoria seguida ante los Medias Rojas de Boston, esta por 9-2. El éxito dejó sin opciones de supervivencia a sus archienemigos históricos y marcó el cierre de temporada para su cerrador estrella Aroldis Chapman.
Max Fried trabajó seis entradas, con seis ponches y una carrera limpia, y fue respaldado por Cody Bellinger al conectar jonrón y producir cuatro anotaciones.
CODY BELLINGER THREE-RUN HOMER
IT’S 8-1 YANKEES! pic.twitter.com/gUQC8CJQb9
— MLB (@MLB) October 1, 2026
Luis García Jr. también firmó un significativo aporte al batear de 5-3 con otro vuelacercas, signo de la oportunidad de los bateadores del Bronx, quienes ligaron de 9-6 con corredores en posición de anotar.
Sonny Gray cargó con la derrota, que tampoco pudieron evitar varios relevistas, entre ellos Garrett Crochet y Garrett Whitlock.
Chapman, sin oportunidad de cerrar un juego ajustado en la serie de comodín, tuvo una entrada de actuación en la que ponchó a los tres bateadores que enfrentó.
Con ese despliegue se convirtió en el primer jugador nacido en Cuba con participación en 10 postemporadas de MLB, y en el segundo de Latinoamérica con 10 o más experiencias de este tipo, solo superado por el legendario panameño Mariano Rivera (16).
¡EL MISIL SIGUE HACIENDO HISTORIA! 🇨🇺
Aroldis Chapman se convierte en el 2do jugador nacido en Latinoamérica en participar en 10 diferentes #Postseason uniéndose a Mariano Rivera. pic.twitter.com/1VjtJcLAZO
— MLB Español (@mlbespanol) October 1, 2026
Además, con los tres ponches recetados llegó a 76 ponches en octubre, para colocarse en el listado histórico de relevistas por detrás de Rivera (110) y Kenley Jansen (94).
Con 38 años, el holguinero cerró una de sus mejores experiencias de las últimas temporadas. A lo largo del tramo regular fijó una efectividad de 1.92 carreras limpias por juego, con 35 salvamentos y 71 ponches en 51.2 entradas.
Sin Cachorros en juego
Las cosas también fueron bien en casa para los Padres de San Diego, al despachar por segunda ocasión sucesiva a los Cachorros de Chicago, esta vez con pizarra de 4-1.
Gavin Sheets conectó jonrón de dos carreras, al tiempo que Xander Bogaerts y Ty France aportaban dos hits cada uno.
Summer’s over, we’re on to October. pic.twitter.com/I4KRWqSyyf
— San Diego Padres (@Padres) October 1, 2026
La ocasión fue propicia para que el relevista cubano Adrián Morejón debutara en la serie lanzando dos entradas en blanco, con un hit permitido, sirviendo de puente hacia los cerrojos de Mason Miller y Jason Adam.
Todo lo contrario sucedió en Atlanta, donde los Filis de Filadelfia lograron equilibrar el pulso con una victoria 4-3 sellada en 10 entradas, que extendió hasta este jueves la definición del trámite.
Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper y Alec Bohm combinaron su poder con jonrones para la causa de los visitantes, mientras que el joven Andrew Painter retiraba a los bateadores de Atlanta durante tres entradas en blanco para quedarse con la victoria.
Well, that was wild pic.twitter.com/FpU4KdGxXo
— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) September 30, 2026
El relevista cubano Raisel Iglesias trabajó un inning por los Bravos, con un hit permitido y sin tolerar carreras.
A la espera de esta decisión, los Medias Blancas se alistan para enfrentar a los Guardianes de Cleveland en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, que arranca el venidero sábado 3 de octubre.
Por su parte, los Yankees enfrentarán con el mismo objetivo a los Rays de Tampa Bay, que cuentan en su filas con los cubanos con el cubano Yandy Díaz y Victor Mesa Jr.
En la Liga Nacional, San Diego pactó su choque con los Cerveceros de Milwaukee —el mejor equipo de la temporada regular con 103 victorias— y los actuales campeones, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, con el cubano Andy Pagés entre sus referentes, aguardan para conocer su primer rival en la ruta hacia la conquista de su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.

NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame.
The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series (also against the Yankees).
But the Bronx Bombers made the short burst of momentum from Contreras feel insignificant when they erupted for six runs in a game-breaking, series-breaking bottom of the sixth inning that sent deafening roars throughout Yankee Stadium and the Red Sox to a 9-2 loss on Wednesday. Those reverberating sounds were a harsh reminder to the Red Sox that this was likely to be their last game of 2026.
With two flat performances in the final two nights of September, during which they were outscored, 18-2, the Red Sox were denied a chance to play in October. It also extended the streak to five straight seasons of no postseason baseball at Fenway Park.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series, and that ended for us tonight,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So it's frustrating. And there's a lot of things you can say, but in the moment, right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it's going to take some time to get over that.”
It will go down as a roller-coaster spring, summer and brief autumn in Boston. There was the 32-46 hole, which the Sox somehow dug out of with a season-altering 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 7 that included a franchise-tying winning streak of 15 games.
Then there was the final month of the regular season, which included injuries to key players and a stunning lack of offense, two themes that carried into the postseason.
“I'm proud of what we accomplished,” said veteran starter Sonny Gray, who took the loss. “Sour taste in your mouth for the ending. But we were left for dead there for a while, and I will definitely remember that run that we went on and what that felt like, because I've never experienced anything like that in my career -- to dig ourselves out of that hole and to put ourselves in this situation, that was a lot of fun.”
For the Red Sox, the fun ended in New York before it even started.
Quite simply, very little went right for the Sox in this two-game sweep at the hands of their rivals, which lacked the drama of last year’s set that went the distance (also won by the Yankees).
“For our season to end the same way that it did last year against our biggest rival, it sucks” said Red Sox lefty Garrett Crochet.
The bottom of the sixth served as a microcosm of the futility and frustration -- the inning that deep-sixed Tracy and his club.
With Contreras creating some energy in the Boston dugout, Tracy tried to add to it by bringing on Crochet for his first appearance in a game since April 25.
Crochet’s quest to get back in time for postseason play after left shoulder woes was a compelling storyline for the Red Sox, but one that didn’t work in real time.
The lefty seemed to get off to a solid start when he struck out Spencer Jones on a sweeper. But catcher Adley Rutschman’s block wasn’t a clean one, and he appeared to hesitate before throwing to first after retrieving the wild pitch. The initial call of out was overturned on replay. Jones then stole second and moved to third on Rutschman’s throwing error.
From there, things devolved. Crochet didn’t get an out and was charged with four runs, though only one of the three hits he allowed was well-struck.
“Personally, to think that I busted my [butt] the past five months, and for it to end that way, on a personal note, it's tough,” said Crochet. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best I could, and I let them down.”
Gray turned in a strong enough start for the Sox, giving up six hits over 4 2/3 innings and leaving with his team down 1-0.
But the offense never quite came around, and the bullpen had a second straight spotty night. And just like that, the season was over.
“Obviously disappointed,” said shortstop Trevor Story. “A lot of thoughts. Proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the [criticism] and everything around, the way this team came together, and really turned the season around to get back into this position is something that was special, and we're not going to forget that. Obviously, it's not about doing amazing things in the regular season. It’s about the postseason.”

NEW YORK – This is only the first checkpoint of a postseason journey the Yankees hope will stretch deep into October. But if they had to choose an opponent to send home first, few would be more satisfying than the Red Sox.
For the second consecutive year, that’s exactly what they did. Their celebration reflected that, with corks popped and bubbly spraying in every direction.
Luis García Jr. hit an early homer and Cody Bellinger delivered a three-run dagger late as the Yankees trounced the Red Sox, 9-2, on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, sweeping the two-game American League Wild Card Series.
“Being able to celebrate with your teammates after a playoff series win, it doesn’t get old,” said left-hander Max Fried. “This is what we start practicing in February for. This is where we want to be. So it’s just about playing our game, having fun, and hopefully we’ve got a couple more of these we can do.”
The victory vaults the Yankees into the AL Division Series against the Rays, with Game 1 scheduled for Saturday at Tropicana Field. The Yankees plan to start either Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodón, pitching coach Matt Blake said.
Following Schlittler’s lead, Fried permitted three hits over six innings of one-run ball, then leaned on the bats to do the rest against the Yankees’ most historic rival. This had been expected to be a low-scoring series, but New York made it lopsided.
“As I said all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us – especially as well as they pitch,” manager Aaron Boone said. “I’m just really pleased with how we played. We’re going to enjoy that, and excited to get our shot at a really good Tampa [Bay] club.”
Imported to supply power with captain Aaron Judge on the injured list, García provided a big fourth-inning swing that represented an overwhelmingly left-handed lineup’s first dent against one-time Yankee Sonny Gray, who was touched for a pair of runs before exiting to a loud chorus of boos in the fifth.
Born in New York and counting himself as a Yankees fan before moving to the Dominican Republic in early childhood, García beamed as he crossed home plate, pointing into the crowd. He hit 30 home runs during the regular season, seven after being acquired from the Nationals in August.
“I only have one word – unbelievable,” García said. “You feel the crowd, you feel the fans. You feel everything right now. This experience for me, it’s unbelievable.”
Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay, then delivered a run-scoring single to greet left-hander Erik Miller in the fifth – the second time in as many nights Miller surrendered a run to the first batter he faced, having allowed Ben Rice’s first of two homers in Game 1.
The Yankees broke it open with a six-run sixth, sending 10 batters to the plate. Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. collected his first postseason RBI, setting up Austin Wells and Ryan McMahon to knock in runs.
“This shows what we can do,” Lombard said. “We’re obviously a great clubhouse, a great group of guys. When everything’s going our way, when we’ve got all our guys competing like we are now, I think we can do a lot of great things.”
Bellinger capped the rally, slugging a Garrett Whitlock changeup into the seats. This time, Boston intentionally walked Rice to face Bellinger. It didn’t work.
“I was very surprised they were willing to face Cody Bellinger, a guy who absolutely thrives with runners in scoring position and has done it his whole career,” Rice said. “Interesting decision.”
Said Bellinger: “That was a cool moment. I feel like I was able to enjoy that one. Home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play, and hopefully we get many, many more this month.”
Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard homered for the Red Sox, who went 26 innings without scoring a postseason run before Contreras’ sixth-inning shot off Fried – a streak that dated back to Game 2 of last year’s AL Wild Card Series in the Bronx.
Given that drought, the Yanks’ firepower was too much to overcome.
“You’re thinking we're going to play closer games,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating.”
Now the Yankees turn their attention to the Rays, who claimed the division by 4 1/2 games during the regular season and won seven of 13 meetings with New York this year.
But October can change everything, and right now, the Yankees are confident they will.
“I know we didn’t win the division,” said Judge, who is hoping to be activated for the next round. “We weren’t the No. 1 seed, got put in the Wild Card. But we’re not trying to make a statement. We’re trying to play our game and take care of business.”

With his team's back against the wall in Game 2 of the Wild Card series against the New York Yankees, Sonny Gray brought his best stuff to the mound. The Boston Red Sox righty, who was sensational during the regular season, is dialed in early, striking out four while allowing just one run on a solo homer across his first four innings of work. And even that is selling him short: Gray hardly ever missed a spot with any of his wide variety of pitches, and all three of his other hits allowed were weak contact that just happened to be well-placed.
But where some might see a crafty veteran — who was, again, one of the best pitchers in the AL this season — motivated to pitch a gem against his former team, Yankees fans saw a conspiracy. Some sleuths on the internet seemed to see a shiny spot on Gray's neck, one that he kept touching in between pitches. Fair or foul? You be the judge.
Is Sonny Gray using illegal substance in start vs. Yankees? The Bronx sure thinks so
Here's what Yankees fans consider to be the smoking gun. Gray clearly has some sort of discoloration on his neck, and he has gone to that spot (or near that spot) pretty regularly throughout this start.
And in baseball's fiercest rivalry, that's enough for accusations to start flying.
So: fair or foul? You can understand how viewers watching at home with too much time to kill between innings might get the wrong idea here. Baseball's problem with sticky stuff at the start of the 2020s was well-documented, so much so that the league eventually felt compelled to crack down on pitchers who were getting right up to (or in some cases just plainly crossing) the line of what's acceptable. Gray spins the ball as well as anybody, and we know he used Spider Tack back when that was still allowed.
Still, I think we need to put the tin-foil caps away here. After all, MLB now mandates hand and glove checks at the end of each half-inning; if Gray were really touching up on sticky stuff while on the mound, wouldn't that show up as he was heading back to the dugout?
It seems more likely that this is just a feel thing, that Gray is touching the same spot in order to try and reestablish grip over the baseball in ways that are totally innocuous. In this day and age, with so many cameras and the league on high alert, it would be foolhardy in the extreme to risk an elimination game on whether or not you get caught in the act. Then again, it would hardly be the first time that subterfuge came into play in this rivalry.

In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Ben Rice and his four hits, two homers, and six RBI, led the charge — but the bottom of the lineup contributed their fair share as well.
In other words, the Yankees played the perfect ballgame last night. Max Fried will be tasked with carrying the momentum into Game 2. Fried's second season in pinstripes has been marred by a couple of IL stints limiting him to just 20 starts and 112.2 innings, but when he's been healthy, he's been just as good as in 2025. He'll be pitching on seven days' rest in Game 2 — his last appearance was an up-and-down start against the Rays, in which Tampa clinched the AL East.
As far as the recent track record against Boston, Fried has been quite effective. He only faced them twice this season: one was a short start from when he was returning from his latest injury, the other an eight-inning masterpiece in April from before the Red Sox got it together under new manager Chad Tracy. In Game 1 of last year's WCS, he provided 6.1 scoreless innings, scattering four hits three walks while striking out six. The Yankees couldn't hold onto the narrow 1-0 lead he had defended, and sabotaged their own comeback effort after loading the bases with nobody out in the ninth inning. None of that was Max's fault, of course. Provided the lineup supports him, an effort like last year's will be more than enough.
Old friend Sonny Gray never caught on with the Yankees in 2017 and 2018, but he'll have no choice but to step up under the Yankee Stadium lights with Boston's season on the line. Over his first season with the Red Sox, the steady veteran turned in yet another outstanding season, leading the AL with 18 wins (don't think that doesn't mean anything to him) and pitching to a 2.72 ERA. That's the thing about the Red Sox' pitching: they have lots of exciting youngsters like Payton Tolle, who pitched last night, but they also routinely get the most out of their veteran pitchers too. Gray faced New York twice in June and pitched well both times. The latter outing was his best start of the season by game score — one hit, one walk, nine strikeouts over 7.1 scoreless innings.
Unsurprisingly, Aaron Boone's lineup for Game 2 is nearly unrecognizable when compared with the Game 1 starting nine. It's a history-making card: according to James Smyth of the YES Network, it's the first time a team has put eight lefty batters — switch hitters not included — in the same lineup in the postseason. The portside octet includes Trent Grisham, who entered late last night for his first action off the IL. Rice will ascend to the leadoff spot, with Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. to follow. Spencer Jones hits cleanup and plays right field ahead of George Lombard Jr., the lone righty to get the start. Jazz Chisholm Jr. draws in at the keystone, Grisham bats in the seven-spot after him, Austin Wells will bat eighth, and Ryan McMahon starts at third and will hit ninth. Naturally, expect plenty of right-handed bats to come off the bench against a lefty-heavy Boston staff once Gray's start concludes.
